# ggmtools

Shared tools for R packages that estimate multiple Gaussian graphical
models (GGMs), currently

* [spikeyglass](https://github.com/mljaniczek/spikeyglass): Bayesian joint
  spike-and-slab graphical lasso (Li, McCormick & Clark 2019), fitted by EM;
* [multiGGM](https://github.com/mljaniczek/multiGGMr): Bayesian multiple
  GGMs by MCMC: G-Wishart with a Markov random field prior (Peterson,
  Stingo & Vannucci 2015), scalable spike-and-slab (scale-multiGGM;
  Shaddox et al. 2018), multi-platform (Shaddox et al. 2020) and the
  multiple graphical horseshoe (mGHS; Busatto & Stingo 2025).

Both packages import ggmtools and re-export what users call, so the
functions are the same objects whichever package is attached and one
downstream script works on fits from either.

Most functions take plain matrices (precision, partial-correlation, score
or adjacency matrices) or vectors of p-values and probabilities, not
fitted objects. So they work just as well with any other estimator, such
as the joint graphical lasso (JGL), the graphical lasso or a random-forest
importance score: see
[Using ggmtools with other methods](https://mljaniczek.github.io/ggmtools/articles/other-methods.html).

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mljaniczek/ggmtools")
```

## What is in it

| What | Functions |
|---|---|
| Shared edge-table format | `edge_index()`, `as_pip_table()`, `diff_edge_table()` |
| Generics with methods in each package | `pip_table()` (long table of PIPs), `pcor_estimate()` (one partial-correlation matrix per group; ggmtools also provides the method for JGL fits) |
| Evaluation against a known graph | `roc_auc()`, `pr_auc()` (tie-correct ROC and PR curves), `plot_roc()`, `confusion_at_threshold()` (TPR, FPR, precision, F1, FDR, MCC), `topk_overlap()` |
| Estimation error and tuning | `relative_frobenius()`, `kl_divergence()`, `ggm_bic()` |
| Edge selection | `bayes_fdr()` (Bayesian FDR from posterior probabilities), `pooled_perm_pvalues()` (pooled permutation null) |
| Matrix utilities | `precision_to_pcor()`, `threshold_to_adjacency()`, `diff_adjacency()`, `upper_tri_to_matrix()` |
| Data | `brca_pi3k`: TCGA BRCA PI3K-pathway expression, Normal vs Tumor (100 x 28 each) |

## Example: differential edges in the TCGA data

`brca_pi3k` holds standardized expression of 28 PI3K-pathway genes in 100
normal and 100 tumour breast samples. With n > p, the inverse sample
covariance gives a simple (unregularized) estimate of each group's partial
correlations.

```{r pcor}
library(ggmtools)

pcor <- lapply(brca_pi3k, function(x) precision_to_pcor(solve(cov(x))))
d <- diff_edge_table(pcor$Normal, pcor$Tumor, threshold = 0.3)
head(d[order(-abs(d$diff)), ])
```

Which of these differences are larger than chance? Permuting the group
labels gives a null distribution of |difference|; pooling it over all
edges gives fine-grained p-values.

```{r perm}
set.seed(1)
X <- rbind(brca_pi3k$Normal, brca_pi3k$Tumor)
diff_score <- function(rows) {
  p1 <- precision_to_pcor(solve(cov(X[rows, ])))
  p2 <- precision_to_pcor(solve(cov(X[-rows, ])))
  abs(p1 - p2)
}
observed <- diff_score(1:100)
null <- replicate(100, diff_score(sample(200, 100)), simplify = FALSE)

pp <- pooled_perm_pvalues(observed, null)
edges <- cbind(diff_edge_table(pcor$Normal, pcor$Tumor, threshold = -Inf),
               pvalue = pp$pvalue, p_adj = pp$p_adj)
head(edges[order(edges$pvalue), c("node1", "node2", "diff", "pvalue", "p_adj")])
sum(edges$p_adj < 0.05)
```

With 100 samples per group and no regularization, no difference survives
the BH correction over all `r choose(28, 2)` edges. The joint estimators
in spikeyglass and multiGGM borrow strength across groups and are the
tools to use for a real analysis; the same two calls then test their
estimates.

A Bayesian method gives posterior probabilities instead, e.g.
P(edge differs). `bayes_fdr()` selects the largest set of edges whose
posterior expected FDR is below a target (tied probabilities are kept
together):

```{r bayes}
prob <- c(0.999, 0.99, 0.97, 0.97, 0.80, 0.40, 0.05)
bayes_fdr(prob, alpha = 0.05)
```

## Example: evaluating an estimate against a known graph

In a simulation the true precision matrix is known. Here, a chain graph on
20 variables, estimated from only 40 samples:

```{r sim}
set.seed(3)
p <- 20
Omega <- diag(p)
Omega[cbind(1:(p - 1), 2:p)] <- Omega[cbind(2:p, 1:(p - 1))] <- 0.3
X <- matrix(rnorm(40 * p), 40) %*% chol(solve(Omega))

Omega_hat <- solve(cov(X))
score <- abs(precision_to_pcor(Omega_hat))   # edge score: |partial correlation|
truth <- threshold_to_adjacency(Omega, threshold = 0)

roc_auc(score, truth)$auc
pr_auc(score, truth)$auc
cm <- confusion_at_threshold(score, truth, threshold = 0.3)
unlist(cm[c("TP", "FP", "TPR", "FDR", "MCC")])
kl_divergence(Omega_hat, solve(Omega))
relative_frobenius(Omega_hat, Omega)
```

ROC and PR curves step only at distinct score values, so sparse
estimators, which tie many edges at exactly 0, get an AUC that does not
depend on the order of the variables. For a sparse estimate, also compare
`pr_auc(..., method = "average_precision")`: the default trapezoid draws a
straight line across a large tied block, which is optimistic.

```{r sparse}
sparse <- score * (score > 0.3)      # e.g. a thresholded or lasso-type estimate
mean(sparse[upper.tri(sparse)] == 0) # share of edges tied at 0
c(trapezoid = pr_auc(sparse, truth)$auc,
  average_precision = pr_auc(sparse, truth, method = "average_precision")$auc)
```

## Edge tables

Every edge table has the columns `i`, `j`, `node1`, `node2` (one row per
pair i < j, in `upper.tri()` order), followed by method-specific columns.
`pip_table()` adds `group` and `pip`. Differential-edge tables
(`diff_edge_table()`, `spikeyglass::diff_edges()`) add `est_g1`, `est_g2`,
`diff` and inference columns, using `lower`/`upper` for intervals.
